claim: The study compiled a global mungbean diversity panel of more than 1100 accessions from three sources: the World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg) genebank mini-core collection, the Australian Diversity Panel (ADP), and the Vavilov Institute (VIR).
source: In this study, we compiled an international effort, reporting a global mungbean diversity panel of more than 1100 accessions derived from (i) the mungbean mini-core collection of the World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg) genebank, (ii) the Australian Diversity Panel (ADP), and (iii) the Vavilov Institute (VIR), which hosts a one-century-old collection enriched with mid-latitude Asian accessions that are underrepresented in other genebanks, many of which were old landraces collected by Nikolai I. Vavilov and his teams in the early 20th century (Burlyaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sources and number of accessions in the diversity panel, with citation to Burlyaeva et al., 2019 for the VIR collection.

claim: The VIR collection contains old landraces collected by Nikolai I. Vavilov and his teams in the early 20th century.
source: In this study, we compiled an international effort, reporting a global mungbean diversity panel of more than 1100 accessions derived from (i) the mungbean mini-core collection of the World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg) genebank, (ii) the Australian Diversity Panel (ADP), and (iii) the Vavilov Institute (VIR), which hosts a one-century-old collection enriched with mid-latitude Asian accessions that are underrepresented in other genebanks, many of which were old landraces collected by Nikolai I. Vavilov and his teams in the early 20th century (Burlyaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript states this historical information about the VIR collection with citation to Burlyaeva et al., 2019.

claim: The final dataset included 1108 samples with 16 wild and 1092 cultivated mungbean.
source: Together with previous data (Breria et al., 2020; Noble et al., 2018), our final set included 1108 samples with 16 wild and 1092 cultivated mungbean.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample composition with citations to previous studies.

claim: A total of 40,897 SNPs were obtained from the genotyping.
source: A total of 40,897 SNPs were obtained.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of SNPs obtained.

claim: 34,469 bi-allelic SNPs with a missing rate less than 10% were mapped on 11 chromosomes and retained for subsequent analyses.
source: Of these, 34,469 bi-allelic SNPs, with a missing rate less than 10%, were mapped on 11 chromosomes and retained for subsequent analyses.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the filtering criteria and number of SNPs retained.

claim: Principal component analysis showed a triangular pattern of genetic variation among cultivated mungbeans.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA, Figure 1C) showed a triangular pattern of genetic variation among cultivated mungbeans, consistent with previous studies (Breria et al., 2020; Noble et al., 2018; Sokolkova et al., 2020) and ADMIXTURE K=3 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the PCA pattern and references Figure 1C, with citations to previous studies showing consistency.

claim: Worldwide diversity of cultivated mungbean can be separated into four major genetic groups: South Asian (SA), Southeast Asian (SEA), East Asian (EA), and Central Asian (CA).
source: Therefore, worldwide diversity of cultivated mungbean could be separated into four major genetic groups corresponding to their geography: SA, Southeast Asian (SEA), East Asian (EA), and Central Asian (CA) groups.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the four genetic groups identified.

claim: The cross-validation error decreased a little after K=4 in ADMIXTURE analysis.
source: As K increased, the cross-validation (CV) error decreased a little after K=4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), where the north group could be further divided (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states the CV error pattern and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phylogenetic analysis suggests CA is genetically closest to EA.
source: Using wild progenitor V. radiata var. sublobata (Wild hereafter) as the outgroup, the accession- (Figure 1D) and population-level (Figure 2A) phylogenies both suggest CA to be genetically closest to EA.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the phylogenetic relationship with reference to figures.

claim: The SEA group is more distant from CA than EA, and SA is the most diverged.
source: The SEA group is more distant, and SA is the most diverged.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the phylogenetic distances.

claim: Outgroup f3 tests show CA shared the highest level of genetic drift with EA, followed by SEA and SA.
source: This relationship is supported by the outgroup f3 tests showing CA shared the highest level of genetic drift with EA, followed by SEA and SA (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The manuscript states the f3 test results with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Pairwise FST and dxy support the conclusion that CA is closest to EA.
source: Pairwise FST and dxy also give the same conclusion (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript states that FST and dxy analyses support the phylogenetic relationship, referencing Figure 2B.

claim: f4 tests strongly reject the case where SEA and CA form a clade relative to SA and EA (f4[SA,EA;SEA,CA]=0.016, Z=9.519).
source: Similarly, the f4 tests (Figure 2C) strongly reject the cases where SEA and CA form a clade relative to SA and EA (f4[SA,EA;SEA,CA]=0.016, Z=9.519) or SEA and EA form a clade relative to SA and CA (f4[SA,CA;SEA,EA]=0.021, Z=13.956), again suggesting EA and CA to be closest.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific f4 statistics with Z-scores and references Figure 2C.

claim: f4 tests strongly reject the case where SEA and EA form a clade relative to SA and CA (f4[SA,CA;SEA,EA]=0.021, Z=13.956).
source: Similarly, the f4 tests (Figure 2C) strongly reject the cases where SEA and CA form a clade relative to SA and EA (f4[SA,EA;SEA,CA]=0.016, Z=9.519) or SEA and EA form a clade relative to SA and CA (f4[SA,CA;SEA,EA]=0.021, Z=13.956), again suggesting EA and CA to be closest.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific f4 statistics with Z-scores and references Figure 2C.

claim: f4 tests suggest SEA and EA form a clade relative to Wild and SA.
source: With regards to the relationship among Wild, SA, SEA, and EA, f4 tests suggest SEA and EA form a clade relative to Wild and SA (non-significant results in f4[Wild,SA;EA,SEA] but opposite in other combinations).
evidence: The manuscript states the f4 test results regarding the relationship among these groups.

claim: TreeMix and f4 tests suggest gene flow between SEA and EA.
source: Notably, both TreeMix (Figure 2A) and the f4 test (Figure 2C, f4[SA,SEA;CA,EA]=0.005, Z=6.843) suggest gene flow between SEA and EA.
evidence: The manuscript states that both TreeMix and f4 tests indicate gene flow, with specific statistics and figure references.

claim: Nucleotide diversity (π) decreased from SA (1.0×10–3) to SEA (7.0×10–4) and EA (5.0×10–4), while the CA group has lowest diversity (3.0×10–4).
source: Consistent with archeological evidence of SA domestication, the nucleotide diversity (π) decreased from SA (1.0×10–3) to SEA (7.0×10–4) and EA (5.0×10–4), while the CA group has lowest diversity (3.0×10–4; Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific nucleotide diversity values for each group and references Figure 2B.

claim: Linkage disequilibrium decays fastest in Wild and then the SA group, followed by other genetic groups.
source: Linkage disequilibrium (LD) also decays the fastest in Wild and then the SA group (Figure 2D), followed by other genetic groups.
evidence: The manuscript describes the LD decay pattern and references Figure 2D.

claim: The out-of-India event happened about 8.3 thousand generations ago (kga) with 75% parametric bootstrap range between 4.7 and 11.3 kga.
source: According to this model, after initial domestication, the out-of-India event (when other groups diverged from SA) happened about 8.3 thousand generations ago (kga) with 75% parametric bootstrap range between 4.7 and 11.3 kga.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific divergence time estimates with confidence intervals from fastsimcoal2 modeling.

claim: SEA diverged from the common ancestor of present-day EA and CA about 2.7 kga (75% range 1.1–4.6 kga).
source: Not until more than 5000 generations later (2.7 kga, 75% range 1.1–4.6 kga) did SEA diverge from the common ancestor of present-day EA and CA.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific divergence time estimates with confidence intervals.

claim: CA diverged from EA very recently (0.2 kga, 75% range 0.1–0.8 kga).
source: CA diverged from EA only very recently (0.2 kga, 75% range 0.1–0.8 kga).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific divergence time estimates with confidence intervals.

claim: The genetic variation of the EA group gradually declines from east to west, accompanied by the gentlest decline of precipitation per unit geographic distance across Asia.
source: Consistent with this model, the genetic variation of the EA group gradually declines from east to west, accompanied by the gentlest decline of precipitation per unit geographic distance across Asia (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the pattern of genetic variation and precipitation decline, referencing Figure 2F.

claim: Mantel's test revealed a significantly positive correlation between genetic and geographic distances for the SA genetic group (r=0.466, P=0.010).
source: Using this idea, Mantel's test revealed a significantly positive correlation between genetic and geographic distances for the SA genetic group (r=0.466, P=0.010), followed by SEA (r=0.252, although not as significant, P=0.069).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific Mantel test statistics with correlation coefficients and p-values.

claim: No significant correlation between genetic and geographic distances was found for EA (r=0.030, P=0.142) or CA (r=0.087, P=0.172).
source: No such association was found for EA (r=0.030, P=0.142) or CA (r=0.087, P=0.172).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific Mantel test statistics showing non-significant correlations.

claim: The southern groups (SA and SEA) together (r=0.737, P=0.001) have a much stronger pattern of isolation by distance than the northern groups (EA and CA, r=0.311, P=0.001).
source: In addition, the southern groups (SA and SEA) together (r=0.737, P=0.001) have a much stronger pattern of isolation by distance than the northern groups (EA and CA, r=0.311, P=0.001; Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific Mantel test statistics comparing southern and northern groups, referencing Figure 2E.

claim: MANOVA of eight bioclimatic variables indicated strong differentiation in the environmental niche space of the four genetic groups.
source: Multivariate ANOVA (MANOVA) of eight bioclimatic variables (after removing highly-correlated ones; Supplementary file 1e,f) indicated strong differentiation in the environmental niche space of the four genetic groups (Supplementary file 1g,h).
evidence: The manuscript states the MANOVA results with references to supplementary files.

claim: PCA of climatic factors shows that PC1 (42%) separates north and south groups and is associated with both temperature- and precipitation-related factors.
source: PCA of climatic factors clearly reflects geographic structure, where the axis explaining most variation (PC1, 42%) separates north and south groups and is associated with both temperature- and precipitation-related factors (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: The manuscript describes the PCA results with specific variance explained and references figures and supplementary files.

claim: Environmental niche modeling revealed distinct suitable regions of six groups except for CA and EAw, whose geographical ranges largely overlap.
source: Environmental niche modeling revealed distinct suitable regions of these six groups except for CA and EAw, whose geographical ranges largely overlap (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the niche modeling results and references Figure 3B.

claim: The SA-SEA transect has the steepest precipitation gradient (slope = 0.21).
source: Despite the SA-SEA transect having the steepest gradient (slope = 0.21), the spread from SA to SEA has been accompanied by an increase of precipitation and did not impose drought stress.
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific slope value for the SA-SEA transect.

claim: The second highest precipitation gradient slope (0.18) is associated with a strong precipitation decrease if the SA group were to disperse to Central Asia.
source: However, the second highest slope (0.18) is associated with a strong precipitation decrease if the SA group were to disperse to Central Asia.
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific slope value for the SA to Central Asia transect.

claim: CA appears to have the shortest time to flowering, the lowest yield in terms of seed size and pod number, and the smallest leaf size in field trials.
source: In the field, CA appears to have the shortest time to flowering, the lowest yield in terms of seed size and pod number, and the smallest leaf size (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: The manuscript describes field trial results and references Figure 4B and supplementary file.

claim: SEA accessions maximize seed size, while SA accessions specialize in developing the largest number of pods.
source: On the other hand, SEA accessions maximize seed size, while SA accessions specialize in developing the largest number of pods (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes field trial results and references Figure 4B.

claim: The QST values of most traits (root, shoot, and whole plant dry weights under control and drought treatments) are higher than the tails of SNP FST, suggesting trait evolution driven by divergent selection.
source: In terms of seedling response to drought stress, the QST values of most traits (root, shoot, and whole plant dry weights under control and drought treatments) are higher than the tails of SNP FST, suggesting trait evolution driven by divergent selection (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes QST-FST comparison results and references figures.

claim: Simulated drought significantly reduced shoot dry weight for all groups, with the effect on SEA being especially pronounced (treatment-by-group interaction effect, F2,575 = 23.55, P<0.001).
source: While simulated drought significantly reduced shoot dry weight (SDW) for all groups, the effect on SEA is especially pronounced (treatment-by-group interaction effect, F2,575 = 23.55, P<0.001, Table 1 and Figure 4D), consistent with its native habitats with abundant water supply (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D and Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific ANOVA statistics and references table and figures.

claim: All groups react to drought by increasing root:shoot ratio.
source: All groups react to drought in the same way by increasing root:shoot ratio (Figure 4D), suggesting such plastic change may be a strategy to reduce transpiration.
evidence: The manuscript describes the drought response pattern and references Figure 4D.

claim: CA consistently exhibits a significantly higher root:shoot ratio.
source: Despite the lack of treatment-by-group interaction (F2,575 = 1.39, P>0.05), CA consistently exhibits a significantly higher root:shoot ratio, a phenotype that is potentially adaptive to its native environment of lower water supply (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D and Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: The manuscript describes the root:shoot ratio pattern with ANOVA statistics and references figures.

claim: Mungbean was not recorded in the 'Classic of Poetry' (Shijing 詩經) dating between the 11th and 7th centuries BCE.
source: The 'Classic of Poetry' (Shijing 詩經) contains poems dating between the 11th and 7th centuries BCE near the lower and middle reaches of the Yellow River. While crops (especially soy bean, 菽), vegetables, and many other plants have been mentioned, mungbean was not recorded.
evidence: The manuscript states the absence of mungbean in this ancient text.

claim: The first written record of mungbean in China is in Qimin Yaoshu (齊民要術, 544 AD).
source: The first written record of mungbean in China is in an agricultural encyclopedia Qimin Yaoshu (齊民要術, 544 AD, Chinese text and translation in Supplementary note), whose spatiotemporal background (~1.5 kya near the lower reaches of Yellow River) is again consistent with our estimated origin of the EA group.
evidence: The manuscript states the first Chinese record of mungbean with reference to supplementary note.

claim: Xiangshan Yelu (湘山野錄, 1068–1077 AD) recorded that mungbean from the southern parts of Asia had higher yield and larger grains than those in northern China.
source: In support of our proposal, Xiangshan Yelu (湘山野錄, an essay collection during 1068–1077 AD) recorded that mungbean from the southern parts of Asia had higher yield and larger grains than those in northern China (Chinese text and translation in Supplementary note).
evidence: The manuscript cites this ancient text with reference to supplementary note.

claim: Tiangong Kaiwu (天工開物, 1637 AD) mentioned that mungbean must be sown during July and August.
source: Similarly, Tiangong Kaiwu (天工開物, 1637 AD) mentioned that mungbean must be sown during July and August (Chinese text and translation in Supplementary note).
evidence: The manuscript cites this ancient text with reference to supplementary note.

claim: South Asia is the probable area of mungbean domestication.
source: Existing archeological evidence suggests that South Asia is the probable area of mungbean domestication, and at least two independent domestication events have been suggested, including Maharashtra and the eastern Harappan zone (Fuller and Harvey, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript states this based on archaeological evidence with citation to Fuller and Harvey, 2006.

claim: At least two independent domestication events have been suggested for mungbean, including Maharashtra and the eastern Harappan zone.
source: Existing archeological evidence suggests that South Asia is the probable area of mungbean domestication, and at least two independent domestication events have been suggested, including Maharashtra and the eastern Harappan zone (Fuller and Harvey, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript states this based on archaeological evidence with citation to Fuller and Harvey, 2006.

claim: Selection of large seed sizes occurred in the eastern Harappan zone by the third millennium BC.
source: The early archeological records suggest that the selection of large seed sizes occurred in the eastern Harappan zone by the third millennium BC and in Maharashtra, dating to the late second to early first millennium BC (Fuller and Harvey, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript states this archaeological finding with citation to Fuller and Harvey, 2006.

claim: Selection of large seed sizes occurred in Maharashtra dating to the late second to early first millennium BC.
source: The early archeological records suggest that the selection of large seed sizes occurred in the eastern Harappan zone by the third millennium BC and in Maharashtra, dating to the late second to early first millennium BC (Fuller and Harvey, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript states this archaeological finding with citation to Fuller and Harvey, 2006.

claim: Mungbean spread to mainland Southeast Asia and has been reported in southern Thailand dating to the late first millennium BC.
source: This pulse later spread to mainland Southeast Asia and has been reported in southern Thailand dating to the late first millennium BC (Castillo et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript states this archaeological finding with citation to Castillo et al., 2016.

claim: The earliest record of mungbean in China was from the book Qimin Yaoshu (齊民要術, 544 AD).
source: Further north, the earliest record of mungbean in China was from the book Qimin Yaoshu (齊民要術, 544 AD).
evidence: The manuscript states this historical record.

claim: Mungbean was not identified in archaeobotanical evidence in Central Asia ranging from several millennium BC to the medieval period.
source: While mungbean is also cultivated in Central Asia today, it was not identified in archaeobotanical evidence ranging from several millennium BC to the medieval period (Miller, 1999; Spengler et al., 2018b; Spengler et al., 2017), suggesting later arrival.
evidence: The manuscript states this archaeological finding with citations to Miller, 1999; Spengler et al., 2018b; Spengler et al., 2017.

claim: Present-day cultivated mungbeans have the same haplotype in the promoter region reducing the expression of VrMYB26a.
source: A recent genetic study revealed that present-day cultivated mungbeans have the same haplotype in the promoter region, reducing the expression of VrMYB26a (Lin et al., 2022), a candidate gene controlling the important domestication trait, pod shattering, in several Vigna species (Takahashi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript states this genetic finding with citations to Lin et al., 2022 and Takahashi et al., 2020.

claim: VrMYB26a is a candidate gene controlling pod shattering in several Vigna species.
source: A recent genetic study revealed that present-day cultivated mungbeans have the same haplotype in the promoter region, reducing the expression of VrMYB26a (Lin et al., 2022), a candidate gene controlling the important domestication trait, pod shattering, in several Vigna species (Takahashi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Takahashi et al., 2020.

claim: The loss of pod-shattering phenotype in cultivated mungbean may have a common origin.
source: This suggests the loss of pod-shattering phenotype in cultivated mungbean may have a common origin and despite the archaeobotanical findings of several independent early cultivations of mungbean in South Asia (Fuller and Harvey, 2006), descendants from one of these cultivation origins might have dominated South Asia before the pan-Asia expansion.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the genetic evidence with citation to Fuller and Harvey, 2006.

claim: Mungbean is an important grain legume in Asia.
source: Mungbean (Vigna radiata [L.] Wilczek var. radiata), also known as green gram, is an important grain legume in Asia (Nair and Schreinemachers, 2020), providing carbohydrates, protein, folate, and iron for local diets and thereby contributing to food security (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citations to Nair and Schreinemachers, 2020 and Kim et al., 2015.

claim: Mungbean provides carbohydrates, protein, folate, and iron for local diets and contributes to food security.
source: Mungbean (Vigna radiata [L.] Wilczek var. radiata), also known as green gram, is an important grain legume in Asia (Nair and Schreinemachers, 2020), providing carbohydrates, protein, folate, and iron for local diets and thereby contributing to food security (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: Mungbean is capable of tolerating moderate drought or heat stress.
source: Among pulses, mungbean is capable of tolerating moderate drought or heat stress and has a significant role in rainfed agriculture across arid and semiarid areas (Pratap et al., 2019), which are likely to have increased vulnerabilities to climate change.
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Pratap et al., 2019.

claim: Mungbean has a significant role in rainfed agriculture across arid and semiarid areas.
source: Among pulses, mungbean is capable of tolerating moderate drought or heat stress and has a significant role in rainfed agriculture across arid and semiarid areas (Pratap et al., 2019), which are likely to have increased vulnerabilities to climate change.
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Pratap et al., 2019.

claim: Using seed proteins and isozymes, previous studies proposed two expansion routes out of India: one in the south to Southeast Asia and the other in the north along the silk road to China.
source: Using seed proteins (Tomooka et al., 1992) and isozymes (Dela Vina and Tomooka, 1994), previous studies proposed two expansion routes out of India, one in the south to Southeast Asia and the other in the north along the silk road to China.
evidence: The manuscript states this with citations to Tomooka et al., 1992 and Dela Vina and Tomooka, 1994.

claim: The Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex civilization north of the Hindu Kush had extensive contact with the Indus Valley Civilization as early as about 4 kya.
source: As early as about 4 kya, the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex civilization north of the Hindu Kush had extensive contact with the Indus Valley Civilization (Dupuy, 2016; Kohl, 2007; Kohl and Lyonnet, 2008; Lamberg‐Karlovsky, 2002; Lombard, 2020; Lyonnet, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript states this with multiple citations to archaeological studies.

claim: By 1500 BC, the 'Trans-Eurasian Exchanges' of major cereal crops had happened.
source: By 1500 BC, the 'Trans-Eurasian Exchanges' of major cereal crops has happened (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: In the Barikot site (ca. 1200 BC-50 AD) in northern Pakistan, diverse crops were cultivated, including those from West Asia (wheat, barley, pea, and lentil), South Asia (urdbean/mungbean), and likely East Asia (rice).
source: The frequent crop exchange is evidenced by archaeobotanical findings in the Barikot site (ca. 1200 BC-50 AD) in northern Pakistan (Spengler et al., 2021), where diverse crops were cultivated, including those from West Asia (wheat, barley, pea, and lentil), South Asia (urdbean/mungbean), and likely East Asia (rice).
evidence: The manuscript states this archaeological finding with citation to Spengler et al., 2021.

claim: In Bronze-age archeological sites north of Hindu Kush, legumes were observed to a lesser extent than cereals, and SA crops were not commonly found.
source: Despite this, in Bronze-age archeological sites north of Hindu Kush, legumes (such as peas and lentils) were observed to a lesser extent than cereals, and SA crops were not commonly found (Jeong et al., 2019; Spengler, 2015; Spengler et al., 2014a; Spengler et al., 2018a; Spengler et al., 2014b).
evidence: The manuscript states this archaeological finding with multiple citations.

claim: Mungbean is commonly grown under rainfed cultivation and depends on the residual moisture in the fields after the primary crop.
source: Mungbean is commonly grown under rainfed cultivation and depends on the residual moisture in the fields after the primary crop, thus responding to water stress (Douglas et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Douglas et al., 2020.

claim: In the south, a temperature range of 20–30°C and annual precipitation of 600–1000 mm is optimal for mungbean.
source: In the south, a temperature range of 20–30°C and annual precipitation of 600–1000 mm is optimal for mungbean (Ha and Lee, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Ha and Lee, 2019.

claim: In Central Asia, the annual precipitation could be as low as 286 mm.
source: In Central Asia, however, the annual precipitation could be as low as 286 mm, greatly below the lower limit required for the southern mungbean.
evidence: The manuscript states this specific precipitation value.

claim: The earliest record of mungbean in China (Qimin Yaoshu 齊民要術, 544 AD) emphasizes its use as green manure.
source: Indeed, the earliest record of mungbean in China (Qimin Yaoshu 齊民要術, 544 AD) emphasizes its use as green manure.
evidence: The manuscript states this historical information.

claim: In Central Asia, mungbean is a minor crop grown with little input, only in the short duration between successive planting of main crops.
source: In Central Asia, mungbean is a minor crop (Rani et al., 2018) grown with little input, only in the short duration between successive planting of main crops (which is also the dry season in Central Asia, Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4) and using residual soil moisture with little irrigation.
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Rani et al., 2018 and references to supplementary materials.

claim: In Uzbekistan, mungbean is often sown in early July after the winter wheat season and harvested before mid-October to avoid delays in the next round of winter wheat and escape frost damage.
source: In Uzbekistan, mungbean is often sown in early July after the winter wheat season and harvested before mid-October to avoid delays in the next round of winter wheat and escape frost damage.
evidence: The manuscript states this agricultural practice.

claim: Fast-maturing accessions are essential for the production system in Uzbekistan.
source: Therefore, fast-maturing accessions are essential for this production system (Rani et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Rani et al., 2018.

claim: Mungbean is a short-day species from the south.
source: Mungbean is a short-day species from the south, and daylength likely limits the window when mungbean could be grown in the north: Chinese texts during the 17th century (Tiangong Kaiwu 天工開物, 1637 AD) specifically mentioned the suitable duration to sow mungbean to control the flowering behavior for maximum yield (Supplementary note).
evidence: The manuscript states this with reference to ancient Chinese texts.

claim: CA accessions have increased root:shoot ratio for drought adaptation, similar to findings in rice, alfalfa, and chickpea.
source: These accessions also have increased root:shoot ratio for drought adaptation, similar to findings in rice (Xu et al., 2015), alfalfa (Zhang et al., 2018), and chickpea (Kumar et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citations to studies in other species.

claim: 290 mungbean accessions were provided by the VIR.
source: A total of 290 cultivated mungbean (V. radiata var. radiata) accessions were provided by the VIR.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of accessions from VIR.

claim: Most of the VIR accessions are mainly landraces collected during 1910–1960.
source: Most of the accessions are mainly landraces collected during 1910–1960 and are considered these accessions as the oldest cultivated mungbean collection from VIR (Burlyaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to Burlyaeva et al., 2019.

claim: DArTseq data of 521 accessions from the ADP and 297 accessions from the WorldVeg mini-core were included in this study.
source: DArTseq data of 521 accessions from the ADP (Noble et al., 2018) and 297 accessions from the WorldVeg mini-core (Breria et al., 2020) were also included in this study.
evidence: The manuscript states this with citations to Noble et al., 2018 and Breria et al., 2020.

claim: The mutation rate was set to 1×10–8 for fastsimcoal2 analysis, which is within the range of mutation rates used in eudicots.
source: This analysis used all sites covered by the DArT tags (including monomorphic sites), and the mutation rate was set to 1×10–8 which was within the range of mutation rates used in eudicots (Barrera-Redondo et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript states the mutation rate used with citations to studies in eudicots.

claim: Climate layers comprising monthly minimum, maximum, mean temperature, precipitation, and 19 bioclimatic variables were downloaded from the WorldClim database version 1.4.
source: Climate layers comprising monthly minimum, maximum, mean temperature, precipitation, and 19 bioclimatic variables were downloaded from the WorldClim database version 1.4 (Hijmans et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript states the data source with citation to Hijmans et al., 2005.

claim: All climate layers from WorldClim were created based on climate conditions recorded between 1960 and 1990 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds.
source: All climate layers available from WorldClim were created based on climate conditions recorded between 1960 and 1990 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds (approximately 1 km2).
evidence: The manuscript states the temporal and spatial resolution of the climate data.

claim: Eight bioclimatic variables were used for analyses after removing highly-correlated ones: Bio1, Bio2, Bio3, Bio8, Bio12, Bio14, Bio15, and Bio19.
source: As a result, eight bioclimatic variables were used for all further analyses, including Bio1 (annual mean temperature), Bio2 (mean diurnal range), Bio3 (isothermality), Bio8 (mean temperature of wettest quarter), Bio12 (annual precipitation), Bio14 (precipitation of driest month), Bio15 (precipitation seasonality), and Bio19 (precipitation of coldest month).
evidence: The manuscript lists the specific bioclimatic variables used.

claim: Phenotyping of 49 accessions was conducted at WorldVeg, Taiwan in 1984 and 2018 and at Crop Sciences Institute, National Agricultural Research Centre, Pakistan in 2015.
source: Among the 52 accessions used for laboratory experiments, phenotyping of 49 accessions was conducted at WorldVeg, Taiwan in 1984 and 2018 and at Crop Sciences Institute, National Agricultural Research Centre, Pakistan in 2015.

The solution of PEG6000 with an osmotic potential of –0.6 MPa was prepared by adding PEG6000 (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) to the nutrient solution according to Michel and Kaufmann, 1973, and pH was also adjusted to 6.0.

claim: The inbreeding coefficient (f) was estimated as 0.8425.
source: To accommodate the possibility that mungbean is not completely selfing, we also applied (Equation 2) QST = (1+f)VB/([1+f]VB +2 VAW) (Goudet and Büchi, 2006), where f is the inbreeding coefficient (estimated by VCFtools as 0.8425), VB is the among-population variance component, and VAW is the additive genetic variance within genetic groups estimated by the kinship matrix using TASSEL software (Bradbury et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript provides the estimated inbreeding coefficient with citations to methods.

claim: None of the f3 tests for admixture gave a significantly negative value, suggesting the lack of a strong alternative model to the proposed relationship among the four groups.

claim: Mungbean cultivation first spread from South Asia to Southeast Asia, then to East Asia, and finally reached Central Asia.

claim: The specific spread route was shaped by unique combinations of climatic constraints and farmer practices across Asia.
source: Combining evidence from demographic inference, climatic niche modeling, plant morphology, and records from ancient Chinese sources, we showed that the specific route was shaped by the unique combinations of climatic constraints and farmer practices across Asia, which imposed divergent selection favoring higher yield in the south but short-season and more drought-tolerant accessions in the north.

claim: In Bronze-age archeological sites north of Hindu Kush, legumes were observed to a lesser extent than cereals, which may be associated with legume's higher water requirement.

Interestingly, archeologists suggested legume's higher water requirement than cereals may be associated with this pattern, and pea and lentil's role as winter crops in Southwest Asia may be associated with their earlier appearance in northern Central Asia than other legumes (Spengler et al., 2014a; Spengler et al., 2018a; Spengler et al., 2014b).

In that case, the SA-SEA divergence time (4.7–11.3 kga) might indicate the divergence between the two climate zones within South Asia rather than the expansion of mungbean into Southeast Asia, which may occur much later.
